1:
Henry reads the reaction in two parts, heart and word. They were out of all patience at the undertaking, having pleased themselves that while Jerusalem lay unwalled they could swallow it up at will, for the strength and safety of the church are the grief and vexation of its enemies; and then they despised the work, which displayed their malice but served the builders, since by reckoning it a foolish undertaking that would sink under its own weight they did not try to obstruct it until too late. Sanballat scorns the workmen, asking what these feeble Jews will do for materials and whether they take the walling of a city for one day's work; Tobiah must show his wit too, for profane scoffers sharpen one another: if a fox go up, not with his subtlety but with his weight, he will break down their stone wall. Delitzsch notes that Sanballat said this publicly, before the rulers of his people and the army of Samaria, and that the four questions must all have the same subject, which rules out reading the second as asking whether the neighbouring nations will leave the Jews to themselves - the sense Ellicott prefers, granting that contempt is not scrupulous or precise. Ellicott adds that the mockery comes afterwards, a general statement made first and expanded later, as often in this book. Clarke observes that Sanballat, as governor, commanded the army and wished to excite the soldiers.

Nehemiah answered none of it but looked up to God, and Henry notes his first petition only asks a hearing: God's people have often been a despised people, God hears all the slights put upon them, and that is their comfort and a reason they should be as though they were deaf. Ellicott notes Nehemiah's habit of turning everything to devotion as he goes, and finds the prayer full of an angry jealousy for the honour of a jealous God. Henry thinks it was spoken rather by a spirit of prophecy than by a spirit of prayer, and is not to be imitated by those taught of Christ to pray for them that despitefully use them; he notes also that the reason given is not that the enemies abused us but that they provoked thee, so the malice of persecutors should offend us as an offence against God. Clarke says plainly that such a prayer, understood literally, is not lawful for any Christian, and is excusable only in a Jew under severe irritation; but he thinks the clauses declaratory rather than precative, since the Hebrew form serves for both, amounting to no more than that what a man soweth he shall reap. Gill likewise denies any private spirit of revenge and makes the words a prophecy rather than an imprecation, grounded on the destruction already threatened against Moab and Ammon. Wesley asks for judgments that would reform the enemies or warn others, God being said to cover sin when he forbears to punish it. Delitzsch keeps to the sense: Nehemiah asked God to give them up for plunder in a land where they would dwell as captives, since they had openly challenged his wrath by despising him in the builders' hearing.

Delitzsch explains that the wall was so far repaired through its whole circumference that no breach was left up to half its height, which Ellicott puts as a wall now continuous to half its height. Clarke finds the reason emphatic in the original, that the people had a heart to work: their hearts were engaged in it, and where the heart is engaged the work of God goes on well. Henry draws two rules, that good work goes on well when people have a mind to it, and that the reproaches of enemies should quicken us to our duty rather than drive us from it; Gill notes that they built on notwithstanding the scoffs and threats.
7:
Henry marks three things in the conspiracy. It was unanimous, men of different interests made one by their opposition to the work of God; it was close, since they promised themselves success from the secrecy of it, saying the Jews shall not know, neither see; and it was cruel, since nothing less than the murder of the workmen would stop the work. He finds no quarrel behind it, no wrong done and none designed, but mere envy and malice: they hated the Jews' piety and were vexed at their prosperity. Ellicott keeps the scale of the thing small. The tribes enumerated were only small parties under the immediate influence of Sanballat, since nothing beyond that would have been likely to occur among fellow subjects of Persia, and though they resolved on an attack without fearing the Persian authority, they soon abandoned the project; the phrase rendered to hinder it he would translate rather to do it hurt.

Delitzsch records the answer plainly: Nehemiah and the superintendents prayed and set a watch day and night to ward off a probable attack. Ellicott would render the last phrase not because of them but over against them, opposite each point of their encampment, and observes that the setting of the watch was accompanied by solemn and united prayer. Clarke draws the doctrine from the pairing, that the strongest confidence in God's protection does not preclude the use of any means of self-preservation his providence has put in our power, the power to will and the use of it being two distinct things. Henry says the same by dividing the verb: Nehemiah looked up, engaging God for him, then looked about him and set a watch, for prayer without watchfulness is slothful and watchfulness without prayer is proud, and either way we forfeit his protection. Ellicott notes that Judah complained of a growing feebleness, especially as so many were diverted to the watches. Wesley adds that they were partly terrified and partly wearied with continual labour, and that the rubbish was more than they could suddenly remove. Henry will not let it pass: can Judah, that warlike valiant tribe, sneak thus? Active leading men have as much ado to grapple with the fears of their friends as with the terrors of their enemies.

The plot was betrayed by the Jews living among the conspirators. Henry credits them with honesty and affection enough to bring the intelligence themselves, and to say it ten times, repeating it as men in earnest; the message is so abruptly expressed that it finds work for the critics, which may be meant to show men out of breath, whose looks made up the deficiency of their words. Clarke calls the verse extremely difficult, notes that the words our translators supply have nothing correspondent in the Hebrew, prefers the Greek sense that they come up from all places against us, and proposes a one-letter emendation giving what they designed against us, which three scholars contend for though no manuscript supports it. On the posting, Ellicott explains that the lower places were the bare places, where the wall was not yet at its due height and enemies could be seen further off, while Henry adds that setting them by families engaged mutual relations to mutual assistance. Then Nehemiah looked: Gill takes this literally, that he viewed the people to see whether they were in their places and armed, while Ellicott judges the appeal was uttered on the actual approach of an attacking party. Henry draws from Remember the Lord, who is great and terrible, that the reigning fear of God is the best antidote against the ensnaring fear of man, and Clarke asks whether the enemies are more terrible or stronger than God, observing that a people fighting for religion, lives and property can never be conquered once they take up the sword.
16:
Henry notices that the builders returned to the wall without laying down their arms, since if one design failed the enemies would be hatching another. Delitzsch identifies the men so divided as Nehemiah's personal retinue, placed at his disposal as governor for official purposes; Ellicott distinguishes these servants from all the house of Judah, and takes the note that the rulers were behind to mean they stood ready to lead the defence. Henry guesses that the two parties changed services at stated hours, which would relieve the fatigue of both and ease the bearers of burdens whose strength had decayed. On the image of working with one hand and holding a weapon with the other, he says it cannot be understood literally, since the work would require both hands, but shows that they were equally employed in both; Wesley calls it a proverbial speech, like saying of a man who pretends kindness that he carries bread in one hand and a stone in the other.

The trumpet answered a plain difficulty, which Delitzsch gives in Nehemiah's own words: the work is great and wide and we are separated upon the wall, one far from another, so that wherever the sound is heard they must assemble to him, for our God shall fight for us. Clarke sets out the danger, that with walls so extensive and the workmen so scattered the enemies might attack them successively; he therefore ordered them to work as near each other as they could and kept a trumpeter always with him. Henry adds that Nehemiah walked round continually to oversee the work, so that he would have the speediest intelligence of an attack, and draws the distinction the arrangement rests on: as workmen they had to be dispersed wherever there was work to do, but as soldiers they had to come into close order and be found in a body, and so should the labourers in Christ's building be ready to unite against a common foe. He observes too that a sword at the side could be carried without hindering labour, and that the word of God is the sword of the Spirit, which we ought always to have at hand.

Clarke explains the last precaution from custom: the country people used to go home to their families after the day's labour, but being now so formidably threatened they were obliged to sleep in Jerusalem, ready to help their brethren. Delitzsch insists the order was given to the labourers on the wall and not merely to the warriors, so that they should remain together at night rather than scatter through the district, and Henry adds the maxim that the strength of a city lies more in its hands than in its walls. Henry presses the last detail too: the spears were held up from twilight to twilight, and while the heat of the business lasted neither Nehemiah nor his attendants went to bed but slept in their clothes, shifting them only for cleanliness or ceremonial pollution; it was a sign their heart was upon their work that they could not find time to dress and undress. The clause behind that reading is a crux. Ellicott calls the washing rendering very improbable, since the words are simply every man his weapon water, rejects the subtler turn that each man's weapon was his water, and prefers supplying the ellipsis, that every man went with his weapon to the water. Delitzsch finds the words very obscure, admitting no tolerable sense whether the water means drinking or washing, and rejects one attempted emendation. Clarke assembles the ancient versions instead: the Latin has every one strip himself for the bath, the Greek omits the clause, the Syriac has none of us put off his clothes for a month each in his turn. Wesley keeps the washing, referring it to cleansing from some impurity befalling them or their garments.
